AI can help explore alternatives, explain unfamiliar ideas, organize evidence and critique a draft. It can also produce confident errors, invented citations, unsuitable dimensions and designs that ignore the real user, material or shop. The student—not the tool—remains responsible for the decision and the result.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A fast-changing area

AI tools, capabilities, privacy practices and policies change quickly. These notes teach durable critical-thinking and documentation habits. **Current teacher instructions and current PDSB requirements take precedence.**

**Last reviewed: October 4, 2026**
:::

## A repeatable student workflow

<ol class="ter-lesson-sequence">
  <li><a href="01-capabilities-limits.qmd">What AI can and cannot do</a> — assign a limited job and separate facts, assumptions and suggestions.</li>
  <li><a href="02-evaluate-output.qmd">Critically evaluate an AI output</a> — test relevance, accuracy, feasibility, bias, accessibility and omissions.</li>
  <li><a href="03-verify-sources.qmd">Find and verify the source</a> — trace a claim to current, original and authoritative evidence.</li>
  <li><a href="04-reproducible-workflow.qmd">Write a reproducible prompt and workflow</a> — preserve criteria, context, inputs, tool/model and settings.</li>
  <li><a href="05-iterate-purposefully.qmd">Iterate with purpose</a> — change prompts because evidence revealed a problem, not just to collect versions.</li>
  <li><a href="06-document-disclose.qmd">Document and disclose AI use</a> — show meaningful versions, decisions, sources, licences and the student's own thinking.</li>
  <li><a href="07-ai-design-audit.qmd">AI Design Audit</a> — critique a flawed fabrication answer, verify it, improve it and defend the final decisions.</li>
</ol>

## Level 4 evidence standard

Adapted from the internal **Documenting AI Projects: Level 4 Quick Guide**:

- define the goal and success criteria before prompting;
- name the tool/model and give it one limited job;
- preserve the prompt or an accessible export after removing personal or confidential information;
- show meaningful versions—normally three or the number set by the teacher;
- record what changed, why, what was accepted or rejected, and what happens next;
- cite sources and licences, and state exactly where AI helped;
- verify facts, measurements, sources, function, bias, inclusion, accessibility, privacy and copyright;
- explain the student's judgement and take ownership of the final result.

This evidence supports Ontario assessment practice: criteria are communicated in advance, feedback improves learning, and evaluation is based on demonstrated student achievement—not on the apparent polish of an AI output.

::: {.ter-curriculum-relevance}
**Ontario curriculum relevance:** This reusable literacy layer supports **TIJ1O** and any **TDJ, TMJ, TCJ, TTJ, TEJ, TGJ, THJ, TXJ, TFJ, or TPJ** project in which students use AI to research, design, communicate, code, model or evaluate. The subject-specific task still determines what counts as valid evidence.
:::
